body.text: Pakistan successfully tested the country’s first indigenously developed air-to-air beyond-visual-range (BVR) missile, Fa’az, on November 3. With the Fa’az test, Pakistan has joined an elite club of countries with the ability to produce BVR air-to-air missiles. The test of the Fa’az will provide the Pakistan Air Force (PAF) with an option to maintain a large stockpile of BVR missiles, ending the dilemma of running out of BVR missiles. It might pave the way toward the development of indigenous mobile medium-range surface-to-air (SAM) systems. Regardless, the Fa’az will help Pakistan effectively and efficiently counter India’s induction of 114 additional Rafale fighters into its air force.

The missile was test-launched from a Pakistan Air Force (PAF) JF-17 combat fighter. According to Pakistan’s military media wing, the Fa’az is equipped with an advanced terminal guidance system and can engage aerial targets at extended ranges. Based on the available imagery, PAF is believed to have tested the imaging infrared (IIR) version of the Fa’az series, known as the Fa’az-IIR. The missile can travel at speed of Mach 3.5 and reportedly its seeker detection range is 40 km, with an overall operational range of over 100 km.

The timing is interesting, and it raises a key question: why did PAF develop and test the Fa’az when it had successfully shot down multiple Indian Air Force (IAF) jets, including the cutting-edge Rafale, on the night of May 6-7, 2025, using Pl-15E radar-guided BVR missiles?

Unlike an active radar-guided missile, an infrared missile relies on the airborne target’s thermal signature for terminal guidance. Fa’az-IIR relies on the launching aircraft’s fire-control radar for mid-course updates and activates its own internal seeker during the final terminal phase to lock onto the target.

This indicates that, if guided by an Airborne Warning and Control System (AWACS) during a BVR engagement, the Fa’az could be used to neutralize a stealth aircraft like the F-35. This seems a realistic scenario as Iranian ground-based air defense systems using an infrared search-and-track (IRST)-based system successfully targeted an F-35 of the U.S. air force a few months ago. In addition, unlike a radar-guided missile, a system guided by infrared seeker is more resistant to jamming.

Beyond stealth fighters, the IAF is looking to operationalize CATS Warrior, an unmanned combat aerial vehicle (UCAV), in the near future. This is part of the IAF’s future planning to integrate unmanned platforms with its manned fighter jets to launch a maximum number of strikes against the adversary. Given the loss of Indian jets during Operation Sindoor, the IAF is expected to implement a new strategy of controlling manned combat platforms such as Rafales as mother ships to control and guide CATS Warrior UCAVs to drop their payload against selected targets in Pakistan. This will allow the IAF to conduct attacks without exposing frontline fighter jets to the PAF kill chain.

As UCAVs like CATS Warriors are indigenously built and have a significantly lower price tag compared to modern fighter jets, the IAF will be able to deploy them in large numbers. Considering this scenario, the PAF requires a large stockpile of air-to-air missiles, which is not possible if Pakistan relies on foreign vendors because of huge price tags and competitive interests. The homegrown Fa’az, therefore, will be a game changer for the PAF to counter the emerging threat posed by the CATS Warrior. Pakistan can maintain a large stockpile of air-to-air munitions that it builds at home. This will not only enhance the credibility of the PAF, thus increasing its deterrence vis-à-vis the IAF, but will also end the PAF’s dilemma of running out of BVR missiles.

Moreover, in a changing threat environment where drones, loitering munitions, and missiles are playing a larger role in conducting strike missions, countries across the world are enhancing the efficacy of their air defense architecture. In light of this, Pakistan, which so far is reliant on foreign-procured air defense systems, is most probably going to use the Fa’az to develop its own first indigenous ground-based medium-range SAM. Many militaries have converted air-to-air missiles for use in ground-based air defense systems. Key examples include the U.S. NASAMS and Indian SAMAR, which use BVR air-to-air missiles in the air defense role.

India is also looking to buy additional 114 Rafales worth $3.24 trillion, which will enhance the IAF’s firepower. The new Rafales will likely be the F4 standard, more advanced than the F3R version currently in service with the IAF. This will likely augment their ability to fight in a heavy jamming environment, thus bolstering the IAF’s combat effectiveness.

Thus the PAF’s combat planes will look to use a combo of radar-guided Pl-15E and Fa’az IIR missiles in the next encounter with the IAF. Evading two different types of modern missiles in an aerial engagement is a daunting task for the IAF. The PAF has already proven its capability against the IAF; equipped with both the Fa’az and Pl-15E, Pakistan’s combat aircraft will subdue Indian fighter jets even more effectively..

The PAF, which is numerically smaller than the IAF, has a policy of using minimalist means and resources to ensure deterrence and operational readiness. Instead of pursuing an arms race, the PAF’s primary focus remains on introducing new technologies to offset the conventional asymmetry it faces. The Fa’az is one of the key initiatives taken by the PAF in response to the evolving threat on Pakistan’s eastern border.
